objectives: Distinguish the rule-making roles of FASB, IASB, IASC, and the SEC.
Contrast principles-based IFRS with rules-based US GAAP across key measurement choices.
Apply the qualitative characteristics of the conceptual framework to evaluate accounting information.

slides.title: The standard-setters — FASB, IASB, and the SEC
slides.body:
Accounting does not self-organize. Every financial statement rests on a body of **authoritative standards** issued by designated standard-setters whose pronouncements accountants must follow. Understanding who those bodies are, how they acquired authority, and what they have built is the starting point for professional accounting.

**The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB)** was created in **1973**, replacing the older Accounting Principles Board (APB). FASB is a private, non-governmental body whose standards carry the force of law in the United States because the **Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)** — created by the Securities Exchange Act of **1934** — has delegated its statutory authority to set accounting standards to FASB. For US public companies, FASB's pronouncements are binding. In **2009**, FASB launched the **Accounting Standards Codification (ASC)**, reorganizing all prior US GAAP into a single, searchable, topic-based structure — Topic 606 for revenue, Topic 842 for leases, Topic 815 for derivatives, and so on. Before the ASC, preparers had to cross-reference hundreds of separate standards, interpretations, and EITF consensuses; the codification collapsed them into one authoritative source.

**The International Accounting Standards Board (IASB)** was established in **2001** as the successor to the **International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC)**, which had been setting **International Accounting Standards (IAS)** since **1973**. The IASB issues **International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS)**, which have been adopted or permitted in more than **140 jurisdictions**, including the European Union (mandatory for listed companies since **2005**), Australia, Canada, and most of Asia. The IASB operates under the **IFRS Foundation**, a non-profit incorporated in Delaware and overseen by a monitoring board of capital-market regulators. Key IFRS include **IFRS 15** (revenue from contracts with customers, 2014, converged with ASC 606), **IFRS 16** (leases, 2016), and **IFRS 9** (financial instruments, 2014).

The **SEC** wears two hats: it is both a regulator of FASB (through its oversight role) and an independent standard-setter for disclosures unique to public companies, via **Regulation S-X** (financial statement form and content) and **Regulation S-K** (non-financial disclosures). The SEC also determines whether foreign private issuers may file IFRS statements without reconciliation to US GAAP — a policy it liberalized significantly in **2007**, removing the reconciliation requirement for IFRS filers.

The **convergence project** — a joint FASB/IASB effort launched at the **Norwalk Agreement of 2002** — aimed to eliminate differences between US GAAP and IFRS. It produced converged standards on revenue (**ASC 606/IFRS 15**, effective 2018) and leases (**ASC 842/IFRS 16**, effective 2019). But full convergence stalled: the two boards diverged on financial instruments and insurance, and formal convergence work was suspended around **2012**. US GAAP and IFRS remain materially different in dozens of areas.

slides.title: The conceptual framework — qualitative characteristics and measurement
slides.body:
Both FASB and IASB maintain a **Conceptual Framework** that sits above the specific standards and supplies the logic for resolving questions the standards do not address. The most recent joint version was issued in **2018** (IASB) and updated by FASB under its own Concepts Statements.

**Fundamental qualitative characteristics** — the two properties without which financial information is useless:

1. **Relevance**: information has **predictive value** (helps users forecast future cash flows), **confirmatory value** (confirms or corrects prior expectations), or both. Relevance is subject to **materiality** — information is material if its omission or misstatement could reasonably influence the economic decisions of users. Materiality is entity-specific; no universal dollar threshold exists, though the SEC staff has discussed 5% of pre-tax income as a rule of thumb, not a bright line.

2. **Faithful representation**: information must be **complete** (all necessary context provided), **neutral** (free from bias), and **free from error** (the description of the phenomenon is accurate, though estimates are inherently imprecise). Faithful representation replaced the older term "reliability" in the revised framework.

**Enhancing qualitative characteristics** — they increase usefulness but cannot make irrelevant or unfaithful information useful:
- **Comparability** — same items treated the same way across entities and periods.
- **Verifiability** — independent observers could reach consensus on the measurement.
- **Timeliness** — available to decision-makers before it loses capacity to influence.
- **Understandability** — clear and concise for a reasonably knowledgeable user.

**The constraint**: **cost** must not exceed the **benefit** of the information.

**Measurement bases** are where US GAAP and IFRS diverge most sharply:

- **Historical cost**: the exchange price at acquisition. Simple, verifiable, and resistant to manipulation — but increasingly irrelevant for long-lived assets held in a changing price environment. US GAAP relies on historical cost more heavily than IFRS.
- **Fair value**: the price that would be received to sell an asset (or paid to transfer a liability) in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date — defined by **ASC 820** (FASB, **2006**) and **IFRS 13** (IASB, **2011**). Fair value uses a three-level hierarchy: **Level 1** (quoted market prices), **Level 2** (observable inputs, no active market), **Level 3** (unobservable, model-based).
- IFRS permits **revaluation of property, plant and equipment** to fair value (IAS 16) and of investment property (IAS 40); US GAAP does not permit upward revaluations of PP&E after acquisition.

**Conservatism** (or **prudence**) — the older principle that accountants should be more ready to recognize losses than gains. The 2018 IASB framework removed prudence as a qualitative characteristic, arguing it conflicts with neutrality; FASB retains conservatism implicitly through the asymmetric treatment of gains and losses (e.g., lower of cost or market for inventory under US GAAP). **ASC 330** governs inventory under US GAAP; **IAS 2** under IFRS. A key difference: US GAAP permits **LIFO** (last-in, first-out) inventory costing; IFRS **prohibits LIFO**.

slides.title: Principles-based vs rules-based — and where the frameworks diverge
slides.body:
The most discussed structural contrast between the two systems is the **principles-based vs rules-based** distinction.

**IFRS is principles-based**: standards articulate the economic objective and the principles to achieve it, then expect preparer judgment in application. IFRS 15 on revenue, for example, states a five-step model and expects entities to apply judgment to identify performance obligations and determine standalone selling prices. There are comparatively few bright-line tests and quantitative thresholds.

**US GAAP is rules-based**: standards historically provided detailed, bright-line rules precisely to reduce preparer judgment and limit earnings management. The old lease standard **SFAS 13** (1976, superseded by ASC 842) defined a capital lease as one meeting any of four quantitative tests (e.g., lease term ≥ 75% of economic life; present value of payments ≥ 90% of fair value). Companies engineered leases to fall just below the thresholds — a structural incentive FASB recognized and partially corrected with ASC 842. The collapse of **Enron in 2001** (which used rules-based structures to achieve off-balance-sheet treatment for special-purpose entities) energized the debate: critics argued that rules invite structuring; defenders argued principles invite manipulation.

**Key remaining divergences** (as of 2024):

| Topic | US GAAP | IFRS |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory costing | LIFO permitted | LIFO prohibited (IAS 2) |
| PP&E revaluation | Not permitted | Permitted (IAS 16) |
| Development costs | Expense as incurred | Capitalize when criteria met (IAS 38) |
| Goodwill | Impairment only (ASC 350) | Impairment only (IFRS 3 / IAS 36) |
| Extraordinary items | Eliminated 2015 (ASU 2015-01) | Never existed |
| Financial statements | 3 balance sheet dates if restatement | 3 balance sheet dates if restatement |

**Revenue recognition convergence** is the clearest success of the convergence project. **ASC 606** and **IFRS 15**, both effective for most entities in **2018**, share the same five-step model: (1) identify the contract; (2) identify performance obligations; (3) determine transaction price; (4) allocate the price; (5) recognize revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied. The standard was developed jointly over a decade and replaced hundreds of pieces of industry-specific US GAAP guidance.

**Who uses what**: the United States, Japan (which has its own JGAAP alongside optional IFRS), and a handful of other countries do not require IFRS for domestic listed companies. The rest of the world — the EU, the UK post-Brexit, Australia, Canada, Brazil, India, Korea, and most of Asia-Pacific — uses IFRS in some form. For a multinational firm, the IFRS/US GAAP gap is an ongoing operational and compliance challenge.

**Professional bodies** enforce the standards in practice: the **American Institute of CPAs (AICPA)** for US CPAs, the **ICAEW** (Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, founded **1880**) for UK Chartered Accountants, and the **ACCA** (Association of Chartered Certified Accountants) globally. The **International Federation of Accountants (IFAC)** coordinates international auditing and ethics standards. Understanding who sets the rules, and why they diverged, is prerequisite knowledge for any advanced accounting or finance work.

question.question: Which inventory costing method is permitted under US GAAP but explicitly prohibited under IFRS?
question.explanation: **LIFO (last-in, first-out)** is permitted under US GAAP (ASC 330) but **explicitly prohibited** under IAS 2, the IFRS standard on inventories. LIFO can reduce reported income in inflationary environments by matching the most recently purchased (higher-cost) units against current revenue, thereby lowering cost of goods sold relative to FIFO. Because LIFO provides a tax benefit in the US (companies that use LIFO for tax must also use it for financial reporting — the 'LIFO conformity rule'), many US manufacturers and retailers adopted it. The IASB prohibited LIFO because it can produce a balance-sheet carrying value for inventory that is severely understated relative to current prices, violating the faithful representation principle. FIFO and weighted-average cost are permitted under both frameworks; specific identification is permitted for items that are not interchangeable. The LIFO prohibition is one of the most significant practical differences between the two systems and a major obstacle to full US convergence, given the corporate tax implications of a forced LIFO-to-FIFO switch.

hints: Think about which method matches the most recent costs to revenue.
IAS 2 has an explicit prohibition — not just a preference.
slides.workedSolution: LIFO (last-in, first-out) is permitted under ASC 330 (US GAAP) but prohibited under IAS 2 (IFRS). LIFO produces lower taxable income in inflation and is embedded in many US companies' tax strategies via the LIFO conformity rule. The IASB banned it because the LIFO reserve leaves the balance-sheet inventory amount severely understated. FIFO and weighted-average cost are acceptable under both frameworks.

question.question: Under IAS 2, a company holds 500 units of inventory with a cost of $40 per unit. The net realizable value (NRV) is $35 per unit. What is the total carrying value of inventory on the balance sheet, and how much impairment loss is recognized? Give the carrying value in dollars.
question.hint: IAS 2 requires inventory to be measured at the **lower of cost or NRV**. Cost = 500 × $40 = $20,000; NRV = 500 × $35 = $17,500. Carrying value = $17,500; loss = $2,500.

question.question: LIFO reserve and cross-border comparison
question.prompt: TechMfg Inc., a US manufacturer, uses LIFO and reports inventory of $120 million and a LIFO reserve of $45 million. Its German competitor, Deutsche Bau AG, uses IFRS (FIFO). A financial analyst is comparing the two companies' gross margins and return on assets. Explain: (a) what the LIFO reserve represents and how to adjust TechMfg's inventory to a FIFO-equivalent basis; (b) why the adjusted comparison matters for the gross margin and asset base; (c) which qualitative characteristic of the IFRS conceptual framework the LIFO prohibition is designed to protect; and (d) what tax consequence TechMfg would face if the US adopted IFRS and it were forced to switch from LIFO to FIFO.

question.question: The FASB's Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) was launched in which year, and what was its primary purpose?
options: 1973 — it replaced the APB and established FASB as the primary standard-setter.
2002 — it was FASB's response to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
2009 — it reorganized all existing US GAAP into a single, searchable, topic-based structure.
2018 — it aligned US GAAP with the revised IASB Conceptual Framework.
question.explanation: The **Accounting Standards Codification (ASC)** was launched in **2009**. Before the ASC, US GAAP was scattered across FASB Statements, EITF consensuses, AICPA pronouncements, and SEC staff guidance — hundreds of separate documents. The ASC collapsed them into one authoritative, topic-based structure (Topic 606 for revenue, Topic 842 for leases, Topic 820 for fair value, etc.), making US GAAP easier to research and apply. It did not change the substantive content of standards; it reorganized the presentation. FASB was created in 1973 (replacing the APB); Sarbanes-Oxley was 2002 but produced the PCAOB, not the ASC; the IASB conceptual framework revision was 2018.

hints: The ASC is about organization, not new rules.
Think of a single searchable database replacing hundreds of individual documents.
slides.workedSolution: The ASC was launched in 2009. It reorganized all existing US GAAP into one topic-based codification without changing substantive rules. Before 2009, preparers had to navigate hundreds of separate FASB statements, EITF consensuses, and AICPA guidance documents. The ASC made US GAAP far more accessible.

question.prompt: In 150 words or fewer, explain the two fundamental qualitative characteristics of the IFRS/FASB Conceptual Framework, and give one concrete example of how each characteristic can fail in practice. Name the specific framework document and at least one standard-setter.
question.rubric: Should identify **relevance** (predictive value, confirmatory value, materiality) and **faithful representation** (complete, neutral, free from error). Concrete example of relevance failure: historical cost of land acquired in 1970 at $500,000 is now irrelevant to current decision-making because it bears no relationship to current value. Concrete example of faithful representation failure: a company omits a material contingent liability from the notes, making the picture incomplete. Should name the FASB or IASB conceptual framework (2018 version acceptable). Bonus for mentioning the four enhancing characteristics (comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability) or noting that 'reliability' was replaced by 'faithful representation' in the revised framework.
